title: Design Ride Sharing
subtitle: Watch a driver's GPS ping become a nearby-car search, a match, a trip, and a price.
learn: Why driver location updates are a huge write stream that belongs in memory, not in the main database
How a grid of cells (geohash or H3) turns 'who is nearby?' into a few cheap lookups
How matching ranks candidates by ETA and avoids offering one driver to two riders
How a trip state machine with guarded transitions survives retries, timeouts and cancellations
How surge pricing is computed per cell from demand and supply, and why it is smoothed

steps.title: Where is everyone, right now?
steps.body: A rider taps Request. Within a few seconds the system must find a nearby free driver, get that driver to say yes, and agree on a price. The hard part is that every driver keeps moving, so "nearby" changes every few seconds. We will build four pieces: a stream of driver locations, a map index that answers "who is close?", a matcher with a trip state machine, and surge pricing.
steps.idea: Ride sharing is a real-time search over things that will not stand still.
steps.caption: A rider wants a car; drivers are scattered and always moving.

steps.title: Drivers report their position
steps.body: Assume 1 million drivers are online at peak, and each app sends its GPS position every 4 seconds. That is about 250,000 updates ("pings") per second, each roughly 100 bytes (driver id, latitude, longitude, heading, time). Pings travel over a persistent connection to the gateway, then to the location service. Losing one ping is harmless because another comes in 4 seconds, so there is no heavy durable write per ping. A sampled copy goes to a log for trip routes and analytics, away from matching.
steps.idea: Location updates are a high-volume stream where only the newest value matters for matching.
steps.caption: GPS pings stream in from driver phones.

steps.title: Index drivers by map cell
steps.body: The location service files each driver into an in-memory index, grouped by map cell. Geohash and H3 are schemes that give each map region a short id (geohash uses rectangles, H3 hexagons); a cell is about a kilometre across. A driver who crosses into a new cell moves to that cell's set. Each entry has a TTL (time to live): a countdown after which it is deleted unless the next ping refreshes it, so a dead app vanishes in about 30 s. The index is sharded (split across machines by cell) to handle 250,000 writes per second. The data is only about 100 MB, so sharding is for speed and availability, not space. A lost shard refills from new pings within one TTL.
steps.idea: Cutting the map into cells turns 'find nearby' into 'read a few small sets'.
steps.caption: Each driver is filed under their current cell and expires if not refreshed.

steps.title: A rider asks for a car
steps.body: The rider sends a pickup and a destination. The gateway checks who they are and forwards the request to the matching service, which creates a ride request. Ride requests are rare compared with location pings: even a big service sees only hundreds to a few thousand per second. That is why the matcher can afford to be careful while the location path must stay cheap.
steps.idea: Ride requests are rare compared with location writes, so the matcher can afford to be careful.
steps.caption: The ride request reaches the matching service.

steps.title: Find nearby drivers
steps.body: The matcher works out the rider's cell, then asks the geo index for free drivers in that cell and the ring of cells around it. Neighbours matter because the rider may stand at a cell's edge, where the closest car is in the next cell. If too few drivers come back, it widens to the next ring. This usually returns a few dozen candidates from a handful of in-memory reads, in single-digit milliseconds.
steps.idea: Search the rider's cell plus neighbours, and widen the ring only if you must.
steps.caption: Candidate drivers come back from the cells around the rider.

steps.title: Rank, reserve, and offer
steps.body: The matcher keeps the closest 10 or so candidates by straight-line distance, then ranks them by ETA (estimated arrival time) from a routing service, since a car across a river may be ten minutes away. It asks the trip service to reserve the best driver. That is a conditional write on the driver's record: "set current_offer to this trip only if the driver is AVAILABLE", in the same transaction that creates the trip as REQUESTED. The reservation expires after 15 s. So no driver is offered two rides. Larger platforms often batch requests for a couple of seconds and match them together; this one-at-a-time version is the simple form.
steps.idea: Rank by ETA, then reserve one driver with a compare-and-set so nobody is offered two rides.
steps.caption: The driver is reserved, a trip row is created, and the offer goes out.

steps.title: The trip state machine
steps.body: Drivers usually take 5 to 10 s to tap accept, so the request is about 8 s old. A trip moves through REQUESTED, ACCEPTED, ARRIVED, IN_PROGRESS and COMPLETED, and can be CANCELLED from the early states. Every change is a guarded update such as "set ACCEPTED only if state is REQUESTED and this driver holds the offer", so retries fail harmlessly. The database is the source of truth, and the trip service then marks the driver busy in the geo index. If every attempt is declined or times out, the trip becomes EXPIRED and the rider is told no cars are available.
steps.idea: Guarded transitions make retries and races harmless.
steps.caption: The accept becomes a guarded state change in the trip database.

steps.title: The driver does not answer
steps.body: Now suppose the driver is in a tunnel and the 15 second timer runs out. The trip service releases the reservation and tells the matcher, which about 1 s later offers the ride to the next candidate. The request is now about 17 s old (1 s before the first offer, a 15 s timeout, 1 s to re-offer). If the first driver's accept arrives late, the guarded update sees the trip is no longer waiting for that driver and rejects it. Each decline adds delay, so many systems cap attempts and then widen the search.
steps.idea: Timeouts plus guarded updates keep a slow driver from corrupting a trip that moved on.
steps.caption: The offer expires, the matcher moves on, and a late accept is rejected.

steps.title: Price from supply and demand
steps.body: When requests far outnumber free drivers in an area, surge raises the price. This attracts more drivers and cools demand. A pricing job counts free drivers per cell from the geo index every few seconds and averages them over a one to two minute window. It also counts open requests from the matcher. It turns the ratio into a multiplier, smooths it and caps it. When the matcher quotes a fare, it asks the pricing service for that cell's current multiplier. The quote is locked for a few minutes, so the price does not change between confirming and matching.
steps.idea: Surge is a per-cell ratio of demand to supply, smoothed and capped.
steps.caption: Supply and demand counts per cell become a multiplier on the fare.

steps.title: The whole picture
steps.body: Pings flow into a sharded, in-memory cell index with short TTLs. A ride request searches the rider's cell and its neighbours, ranks by ETA, reserves one driver, and offers the ride with a timeout. A guarded state machine in the trip database keeps every change safe under retries. Surge turns per-cell supply and demand into a price. Only the few decisions that matter touch the durable database.
steps.idea: Keep the hot stream in memory, and put strong guarantees only on the small set of decisions that need them.
steps.caption: Ingest, index, match, trip, price.

quiz.q: Why is the live driver location store usually an in-memory index with a TTL instead of rows in the main trip database?
options: Relational databases cannot index latitude and longitude at all
Each position is overwritten within seconds, so durability is wasted and the write rate is huge
Location data is too sensitive to ever be written to disk
In-memory stores guarantee no two riders get the same driver
quiz.why: Only the latest position matters and a new one arrives every few seconds. Durable storage would pay a high cost to keep data that is stale for matching almost immediately. A TTL also removes drivers whose apps went silent.

quiz.q: A rider stands right on the boundary between two grid cells. What must the nearby-driver search do?
options: Search only the rider's own cell, since it contains the rider
Search every cell in the city
Ask drivers to report which rider is closest
Search the rider's cell and its neighbouring cells
quiz.why: The nearest car may sit just across the cell edge. Checking the cell plus its neighbours fixes that cheaply, and the ring widens only if too few drivers are found.

quiz.q: Two riders are matched to the same best driver at the same moment. Which design stops both from getting the trip?
options: Send both offers and let the driver pick
Make the geo index fully consistent across regions
Reserve the driver with a conditional update that succeeds for only one request
Cache the driver list for longer
quiz.why: A compare-and-set on the driver's record (set current_offer only if the driver is AVAILABLE) lets exactly one request win. The loser sees the condition fail and tries the next candidate. The index is only a hint, so the guarantee must live in the store holding that record.

quiz.q: A driver's accept message arrives 20 seconds after the 15-second offer window closed and the trip was given to another driver. What should happen?
options: Accept it and reassign the trip
Reject it because the guarded update finds the trip is no longer in the expected state for that driver
Accept it and cancel the other driver
Ignore it silently and leave the driver waiting
quiz.why: State transitions are conditional on current state and owner, so a stale message cannot change a trip that moved on. The driver should be told the offer is gone so their app returns to idle.

quiz.q: Why is surge computed per cell over a window and then smoothed, instead of using the raw request count each second?
options: Averaging over a window is needed because the index only stores counts per day
Raw counts cannot be compared between cells of different sizes
Per-second ratios swing wildly and would make prices flicker
It lets the index skip TTLs
quiz.why: Short windows are noisy: one burst of requests would spike prices and then drop them seconds later. A one to two minute window with smoothing and a cap gives stable, explainable prices.

cheatsheet.def: Ways to cut the map into cells with ids. Nearby places share a cell or neighbouring cells, so a spatial search becomes a lookup by id.
Query the rider's cell, then its neighbours, then wider rings only if too few drivers are found.
Each driver entry expires after about 30 seconds, so silent or crashed apps drop out of the index on their own.
1M online drivers pinging every 4 s is about 250k writes/s at roughly 100 bytes each, around 25 MB/s. Rule of thumb, not a measured figure.
Rank candidates by estimated drive time on roads, not straight-line distance, since rivers and one-way streets change the answer.
Fixed states (REQUESTED, ACCEPTED, ARRIVED, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED, CANCELLED, EXPIRED) with conditional updates so only valid moves succeed.
A compare-and-set on the driver's availability that holds one driver for one request for a short lease, preventing double offers.
Fare factor from demand versus supply per cell over a sliding window, smoothed and capped to avoid flicker.

lab.prompt: Design the backend for a ride-sharing service in one city of 200,000 online drivers at peak. Cover how location updates are ingested, how nearby drivers are found, how a driver is matched and a trip tracked, and how surge is priced. State your numbers and where each piece of data lives. Assume each driver pings every 4 seconds and the city sees about 100 to 300 ride requests per second at peak.
requirements: Ingest driver location updates and make them searchable within a few seconds.
Return nearby free drivers for a pickup point in under 100 ms.
Never assign one driver to two active trips.
Handle driver decline, timeout, and late messages without corrupting trip state.
Define the trip states and the allowed transitions.
Compute a per-area surge multiplier that does not flicker.
Estimate write rate, memory for the index, and ride requests per second.
hints: Work out pings per second first: drivers divided by the ping interval. Then size the index by entries times bytes per entry.
Pick a cell size so a typical cell holds a handful of drivers, and decide how many rings you will search.
Put the location index in memory with a TTL, and the trip record in a durable database with a version column.
Write the reservation and each transition as a conditional update, and think about what happens if the same request is sent twice.
For surge, count requests and free drivers per cell over a window, take the ratio, then smooth and cap it.
checklist: Location writes go to an in-memory, sharded index with a TTL, not the trip database.
Nearby search checks the rider's cell plus neighbouring cells.
Candidates are ranked by ETA and offered one at a time with a timeout.
Reservation is a compare-and-set on driver availability, and state changes use conditional updates, so a second assignment fails.
States and transitions are listed, including cancellation.
Surge is per cell, windowed, smoothed, and capped.
Numbers are stated: pings per second, index size, requests per second.
